issues.legal_issue: Taking possession under an urgent acquisition before publication of the declaration vests the land in the State and prevents the acquisition from lapsing for failure to make an award within the prescribed period.
material_facts: An urgency procedure was invoked and the enquiry ordinarily available to affected persons was dispensed with.
After notice was served, possession was taken before publication of the declaration, and a pumping station was constructed.
The purchaser acquired the land after publication of the acquisition notice.
No notice withdrawing the land from the acquisition was published.
issues.conclusion: The land vested in the State when possession was taken under the urgency procedure, the acquisition did not lapse, and the later purchaser could not challenge the acquisition or the regularity of taking possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(2) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, possession taken after the prescribed notice in an urgent acquisition vests the land in the State free from encumbrances. Section 11A does not cause such an acquisition to lapse after vesting; withdrawal under Section 48(1) is the relevant means of withdrawing from the acquisition. A transfer made after publication of the Section 4(1) notification does not bind the State, and the purchaser acquires no title with which to challenge the notification or possession.

rule.if: urgent_acquisition_proceeding and possession_taken_after_notice_before_declaration and no_withdrawal_notice and later_purchaser_challenges_acquisition

predicates.urgent_acquisition_proceeding: The acquisition authority proceeds on an asserted urgent need and dispenses with the ordinary enquiry.
predicates.possession_taken_after_notice_before_dec: The authority takes possession after serving the required notice but before publishing the acquisition declaration.
predicates.no_withdrawal_notice: The authority does not publish a notice withdrawing the land from the acquisition.
predicates.later_purchaser_challenges_acquisition: A person who acquired the land after the initial acquisition notice challenges the acquisition or the taking of possession.

issues.definition: When an urgent acquisition proceeds to possession after notice and is not withdrawn, a later purchaser's challenge does not undo the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who acquires land after the acquisition notice has no title to the land but may claim the compensation payable to the former owner under the acquisition law.
material_facts: The respondent purchased the land after the acquisition notice had been published.
The respondent sought compensation for the acquired land.
The original owner was entitled to compensation, and the respondent claimed through that interest.
issues.conclusion: Although the respondent acquired no title against the State, it could claim compensation as a person interested by stepping into the former owner's shoes, subject to the acquisition law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides for compensation to the owner or person interested. A purchaser who acquires after publication of the acquisition notice takes no title against the State but may claim the compensation interest of the former owner. The market value is assessed as at publication of the Section 4(1) notification.

predicates.compensation_claim_proceeding: A claimant seeks compensation for land taken in an acquisition.
predicates.later_purchaser_claims_for_acquired_land: A person who acquired the land after the acquisition notice seeks compensation for that land.

issues.definition: A later purchaser seeking compensation for acquired land may claim through the former owner's compensation interest, despite having no title against the State.

issues.legal_issue: A basic valuation register maintained for stamp-duty purposes cannot, by itself, establish the market value of acquired land for compensation.
material_facts: The Collector assessed compensation using rates in government basic valuation circulars used for stamp duty.
The High Court directed payment on the basis of that assessment.
The valuation was not founded on evidence of the prevailing market value of the particular land.
issues.conclusion: The Collector's stamp-duty-based valuation was legally erroneous and could not provide the foundation for determining compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value must be determined from evidence adduced by the claimant and rebuttal evidence adduced by the State. In Jawajee Nagnatham v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Adilabad, A.P. & Ors. (1994) 4 SCC 595, the Court held that a basic valuation register maintained for stamp-duty collection cannot form the foundation for determining market value. State of U.P. & Ors. v. Shau Singh (1995 HVD Vol. I 191) likewise held that stamp-duty rates cannot be relied on to determine market value.

predicates.compensation_valuation_proceeding: A court or authority is determining compensation for acquired land.
predicates.stamp_duty_schedule_used_as_market_value: A valuation schedule maintained for collecting stamp duty is used as the basis for fixing the land's market value.

issues.definition: In compensation valuation, using a stamp-duty schedule as the market-value basis does not establish the value of the acquired land.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation must reflect the land's market value at the acquisition-notice date and account for its condition and the scale of the acquisition, rather than later development or an unsupported square-foot rate.
material_facts: The land was acquired to drain flood water from a low-lying area and was not developed at the relevant time.
The Collector's assessment used a later valuation and a rate per square foot, which the Court found unsupported as a basis for compensation.
The acquisition covered a large area, for which valuation by yardage and a deduction for development requirements were relevant.
A later purchase price for the property was placed before the Court, and subsequent development of the area was also discussed.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the Collector's valuation and fixed total compensation at Rs. 25,000, with 15% solatium and 6% interest from possession until deposit, rather than remitting the matter for fresh valuation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires market value to be determined as at publication of the Section 4(1) notification. Under Section 24, subsequent development is irrelevant to that determination. For a large acquisition, valuation should be on a yardage basis rather than a square-foot basis, with a deduction for land required for development. A sale may provide a basis for valuation if it is a bona fide transaction between willing parties in normal market conditions and was not intended to inflate the value of the acquired land.

rule.if: compensation_appeal and acquired_land_was_undeveloped_at_notice_date and large_area_acquired and later_development_relied_on

predicates.compensation_appeal: An appeal concerns the amount of compensation awarded for acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_was_undeveloped_at_notice_: The land had not been developed when the acquisition notice was published.
predicates.large_area_acquired: The acquisition covered a large tract of land.
predicates.later_development_relied_on: A party relies on development occurring after the acquisition notice to support the land's market value.

issues.definition: For a compensation appeal involving a large, undeveloped tract, the award must reflect market value at the notice date, with relevant area and development adjustments, rather than later development.
